landscape: Public opinion data are abundant. The domain has a stable core of academic survey programmes. In the United States the core is ANES, the GSS and the Cooperative Election Study. Across countries it is the World and European Values Surveys, the European Social Survey, ISSP, CSES and the regional barometers (Afro-, Arab, Asian, Americas, Latino and Caucasus). Around them sit national election studies, now running in dozens of democracies, and household and internet panels with political modules (LISS, GIP, GESIS Panel, Understanding Society, SOEP).

Two developments define the last decade. The first is the growth of very large opt-in online samples and panels (CES, Nationscape, the BES Internet Panel, Pew's American Trends Panel). These allow analysis of states, small groups and short time spans, but they rely on weighting rather than probability sampling. The second is the spread of harmonised and latent measures that pool many surveys into comparable series: Survey Data Recycling, the Integrated Values Surveys, Claassen's democratic mood, the policy-mood and macropartisanship series, and subnational ideology estimates.

Access varies widely in this domain. Most academic surveys are open or need free registration, and many are distributed through national archives such as GESIS, the UK Data Service, ICPSR and CDSP, which this catalog lists as infrastructure portals. Several important collections are licensed or restricted: Roper iPoll, the Gallup World Poll, the Asian Barometer, merged AmericasBarometer files and the Indian National Election Study. Gallup ended its presidential approval series at the start of 2026.

core.text: The American National Election Studies have interviewed probability samples of American citizens before and after every presidential election since 1948, adding panels, pilot studies and a cumulative file. The 2024 study has about 5,500 pre-election and 5,000 post-election interviews. It is a standard source on U.S. voting behaviour and partisanship. Sample sizes limit state-level and small-group analysis, and self-reported turnout is inflated relative to validated records.

The Cooperative Election Study (formerly CCES) surveys about 60,000 Americans each election year since 2006 through a matched opt-in online sample. Team modules sit on a common core, and a cumulative file holds over 700,000 respondents. Its size makes state, district and subgroup analysis possible, but it relies on matching and weighting rather than probability sampling, and its validated-vote measures depend on commercial voter files.

The World Values Survey has measured values on religion, family, work, politics and democracy in seven waves since 1981, reaching 66 countries in Wave 7 (2017-2022). Together with the European Values Study it provides a long-running cross-national series on mass values. Country participation is uneven across waves, and fieldwork within a wave spans several years.

The European Social Survey has interviewed probability samples across Europe every two years since 2002, with rigorous standards for sampling, translation and documentation. Its rotating modules cover political trust, participation and attitudes to democracy, immigration and welfare. It is a common benchmark for cross-national survey quality in Europe. The transition to self-completion modes in Rounds 12-13 creates a series break.

The Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (renamed the Comparative Study of Election Surveys in 2026) fields a common module in national post-election studies. The Integrated Module Dataset harmonises about 396,000 respondents from 230 elections in 59 polities. It is designed for studying how institutions shape voting behaviour, though coverage is tilted towards established democracies.

choosing: Choose between probability samples and large opt-in samples according to the estimand. Population descriptions and long trends favour probability designs (ANES, GSS, ESS). Subgroup, state and short-term dynamics favour very large online samples (CES, Nationscape, panels), provided weighting and representativeness are checked.

For cross-national work, prefer harmonised resources (CSES IMD, SDR2, the Integrated Values Surveys) over pooling raw barometers, whose question wordings and response scales differ. Always cite the specific wave, module or release used, since most programmes revise weights and files after first release.
gaps: National election studies with an identifiable official home are missing for several Central and Eastern European democracies (only listed by the CNES knowledge bank), and the Turkish Election Study has no archived full dataset.
South Asian, Middle Eastern and many African national opinion data remain restricted or available only as tables, so cross-national work relies on the regional barometers.

Several long-running series have ended or changed design recently: Gallup's presidential approval series (2026), FiveThirtyEight's polls archive, TESS, and the ESS mode switch, all of which create breaks for trend analysis.
